one_liner: In-place, stable, adaptive C sort beating std::stable_sort via rotations instead of an O(n) swap buffer.
what_it_does: Blitsort is a stable sort for C that uses O(1)-ish auxiliary memory (a small fixed or sqrt(n) swap buffer plus O(log n) recursion stack) instead of allocating O(n) scratch space like a classic merge sort. It combines rotate mergesort and rotate quicksort variants of the author's quadsort/fluxsort/crumsort family, picked by an analyzer that scans how ordered the input already is. The API mirrors qsort() (array, nmemb, size, cmp) rather than std::sort's template/iterator interface, with type-specialized entry points (blitsort8/16/32/64/128) and a blitsort_prim() path for branchless 32/64-bit integer sorts without a comparator.
how_it_is_fast: Two custom primitives do most of the work: a 'trinity rotation' (the author's own array-rotation algorithm, described as significantly faster than standard triple-reversal rotation) used to move partitions in place instead of copying to a swap buffer, and a 'monobound binary search' used to locate rotation points, claimed up to 2x faster than a typical binary search. An analyzer detects already-sorted, reverse-sorted, and mostly-sorted runs up front and routes them to rotate quadsort/fluxsort fast paths. On primitive types, uncommenting the `cmp` macro (or defining it before include) switches to branchless comparisons, which the README says roughly doubles throughput.
when_to_use: Need a stable sort in C with a small, bounded auxiliary-memory footprint (no O(n) swap buffer) rather than std::stable_sort's allocation.

Input has structure (ascending/descending runs, sawtooth, pipe-organ, partially sorted tails) — the adaptive analyzer gives the largest wins here (README table: ~17x on 100K descending 32-bit ints vs std::stable_sort).
Sorting primitive 32/64-bit integers, doubles, or long doubles, or larger records via pointer indirection (e.g. strings) under a qsort-compatible call site.
Codebase can vendor a small C source drop (blitsort.h/.c + bundled quadsort.h/.c) rather than link a library, and wants roughly 2.5x throughput over libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random 64-bit data.
Migrating qsort() call sites incrementally without adopting a templated/iterator C++ API.
when_not_to_use: 128-bit / long double keys: the README's own table shows blitsort roughly at parity with std::stable_sort on random order (0.011423s vs 0.011047s avg) and clearly behind pdqsort/crumsort there.

'Ascending tiles' and 'bit reversal' distributions: blitsort is measurably slower than std::stable_sort in the README's own data (0.001397s vs 0.000948s; 0.002160s vs 0.001355s), so gains aren't universal.
Stability isn't required and raw speed on plain random order is the goal: the README's own benchmark shows pdqsort and crumsort both beating blitsort on random-order 32/64-bit ints.
Need a modern templated/iterator C++ API, exceptions, or custom allocator support: blitsort is a C, qsort()-signature function, not a std::sort drop-in.

Want active upstream maintenance or CI/test coverage signals: last commit 2024-07-27, no CI config visible in the tree, and the published benchmarks run on gcc 7.5.0 inside WSL2 with no bare-metal CPU model given.

integration.dependencies: quadsort.c/quadsort.h (bundled in src/, required include); otherwise only the C standard library
integration.min_toolchain: not documented precisely; header uses <stdalign.h> (C11) and assert/errno/string/stdio/float.h; README benchmarks built with gcc 7.5.0 / g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive
integration.platforms: any (portable C, no intrinsics in the public API); all published benchmarks are x86-64 under WSL2, no other platform data given
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — matches qsort(void*, size_t, size_t, CMPFUNC*) exactly, but std::stable_sort callers need an adapter since there is no template/iterator API

gotchas: Full branchless speedup requires manually defining the `cmp` macro before including blitsort.h (or editing bench.c); without it, primitive comparisons go through a function pointer and the README says throughput roughly halves.
blitsort_prim() only supports 32/64-bit signed/unsigned integers (size codes 4/5/8/9); other sizes hit an assert.

blitsort() itself only dispatches sizes matching char/short/int/long long/long double; any other element size falls through to an assert rather than a qsort() fallback (that fallback line is commented out in blitsort.h).
'In-place' is the loose community definition: it still uses up to 512 elements of swap memory by default (configurable down to 32 or sqrt(n)) plus O(log n) recursion stack, not strict O(1).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick blitsort over its own siblings quadsort/fluxsort when you need stability but can't spare their O(n) auxiliary buffer, and over crumsort/pdqsort when stability is required (both are unstable, and crumsort is faster than blitsort on plain random-order data per the README's own pdqsort/crumsort table). Pick fluxsort or quadsort instead when O(n) scratch memory is available and stability plus a bit more raw speed matters more than memory footprint.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's wolfsort harness (g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive, WSL2 gcc 7.5.0, libstdc++'s std::stable_sort as baseline), blitsort sorted 100,000 random-order 64-bit ints in avg 0.002518s vs 0.006207s for std::stable_sort (~2.5x) and 32-bit ints in 0.002341s vs 0.006025s (~2.6x); gains are far larger on structured distributions (e.g. ~17x on descending order) but shrink to roughly parity on 128-bit long doubles. No CPU model was reported for the runs.
status_note: Stale since the last commit on 2024-07-27 (0 open issues, all 5 historical issues closed with no unresolved bugs), but Unlicense (public domain, no patent grant) and a small qsort-compatible C source make it cheap to vendor and freeze at a known-good commit.
